strengths: Addresses a useful finite-length coding problem: constructing high-rate quaternary codes for single insertion, deletion, or substitution errors. Using learned embeddings to guide construction of explicit codebooks is an interesting application.
Algorithm 1 has a sound correctness foundation: exact removal of radius-2 Levenshtein neighborhoods ensures minimum distance at least 3, independently of embedding accuracy.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements over random greedy search across ten runs, with average codebook-size gains of 6.4–15.8%. The best length-11 code contains 36,368 codewords, achieving a rate of approximately 68.9%. The loss-function ablation provides additional useful evidence.

The decoder achieves zero observed failures in 100 million random single-edit trials when querying four neighbors, and substantially improves runtime over the implemented brute-force baseline. Clear pseudocode, synthetic data generation, and a source-code link support accessibility.
weaknesses: The central justification for the search criterion is incorrect as stated. Batch normalization does not make embeddings jointly Gaussian. Even under Gaussianity, pointwise density does not establish the number of radius-2 Levenshtein neighbors remaining during greedy search, or guarantee maximum codebook size. The binary t-SNE visualization does not validate these assertions; direct measurements against exact neighborhood sizes are needed.

The advertised O(n) decoding complexity is not established. Exact nearest-neighbor search in a 64-dimensional k-d tree does not unconditionally take O(log |C|) time. Figure 5 shows k=1 runtime increasing from 6 to 367 seconds as n increases from 7 to 11, providing little empirical support for linear scaling. Moreover, k=1 has measurable decoding errors, while the verified multi-neighbor variant is assigned O(n²) complexity by the paper itself.

The decoding comparison is too weak to establish the claimed efficiency advantage. Brute-force comparison against every codeword is not the only exact alternative: one-edit neighborhood lookup tables and bounded-distance search are natural baselines for these short codebooks. The cited hardness of unrestricted edit-distance computation does not establish a comparable lower bound for checking whether two strings differ by at most one edit.

The optimality claim substantially exceeds the evidence. Matching a proposed redundancy curve over a few short lengths supplies neither a converse nor an optimality certificate. At n=11, the substitution sphere-packing bound permits approximately 123,361 codewords, versus 36,368 obtained here. This bound may be loose for IDS correction, but the remaining factor of approximately 3.4 illustrates why it cannot certify the claimed near-optimality.

Construction comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution of learning. Random ordering is the principal search baseline; degree-based, lexicographic, or other combinatorial greedy orderings are absent. Comparisons with asymptotic redundancy expressions also need explicit finite-length codebook cardinalities to substantiate superiority at these very short lengths. The relationship to established greedy code construction is insufficiently developed.

Reproducibility and resource accounting are incomplete in the manuscript. Training-pair sampling, optimizer and schedule, detailed architecture, hardware, and construction costs are insufficiently specified. Enumerating and embedding all 4^n candidates is substantial even within the intended short-length regime, yet construction time and peak memory are not reported.

The experiments establish performance on isolated, already segmented single-edit inputs. They do not establish the motivating gains for concatenated streams with unknown segment boundaries, synchronization failures, and outer-code overhead. Additionally, random decoding trials provide strong empirical evidence but do not certify correction of every single-edit outcome; exhaustive validation appears feasible at the reported codebook sizes.
